newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's Berisha to meet EU team, halts offensive.
newsitem.headline: Albania's Berisha to meet EU team, halts offensive.

text.p: President Sali Berisha made concessions to Albania's opposition, halting a military drive against rebels as a European Union team was due to arrive on Friday to seek a political solution to the unrest in the south.

Berisha held a five-hour meeting on Thursday with his ruling Democratic Party and nine opposition groupings that produced an agreement to suspend operations against the heavily armed rebels in the south for 48 hours.
The rebels, in turn, were offered an amnesty if they handed in their weaponry beginning at 6 a.m. (0500 GMT) on condition they had committed no crimes.

There was no indication rebels in the Adriatic port of Vlore and other southern towns under their control would abide by such an accord, even if it was signed by political opponents of a government whose replacement they have demanded.
Many of the rebels vowed to maintain their armed campaign until Berisha, re-elected to a second five-year term this week by a parliament dominated by his Democrats, stepped down.
"This is a popular uprising and won't stop until Berisha resigns," former army officer Davar told an evening rally in the main square of the port of Sarande -- in violation of a curfew.

Dutch Foreign Minister Hans Van Mierlo held talks on his way to Tirana in Rome and Athens -- the two capitals most directly concerned by any flood of migrants if order broke down in Albania. He believed Berisha was giving ground.
"It is not a matter of if but when," Van Mierlo, whose country currently holds the EU's rotating chairmanship, told reporters in Athens.
Van Mierlo is the first senior Western minister to visit Albania since it imposed emergency rule on Sunday to quell the unrest in the south of the country.

Berisha last week suggested early elections within 45 days to opposition parties and pledged to step down if his rightists lost power. The opposition said that, given the climate of turmoil and suspicion, the time frame was too short.
International pressure has mounted on Albania to take swift action. A Council of Europe delegation was already in Tirana.

Berisha issued a decree enacting the amnesty after his talks with 10 political parties. He also pledged to seek a political consensus on replacing Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi, who stepped down last weekend.
State television said the Defence Council, which oversees emergency regulations, had ordered a suspension of military action in southern areas.
At least 16 people have died in the past week, most in Vlore, focal point of protests that first erupted last month by investors who lost savings in failed pyramid investment schemes.
State television showed other towns in the country of 3.4 million with shops and factories functioning normally.
Italy said it would send back Albanians who crossed the Adriatic Sea to escape the violence. Twenty-nine people who arrived by boat on Wednesday would probably be returned by ferry.

U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Thursday there were no plans for the withdrawal of American diplomats from Albania and "we're not planning right now an evacuation of American citizens".
"The U.S. ambassador (in Tirana) has not requested any kind of military assistance," Burns said.
U.S. military commanders stationed in Germany reported earlier on Thursday that they were making plans to evacuate more than 1,600 Americans living in Albania.

Burns welcomed Berisha's decision to suspend military action against the rebels in the south and said the United States hoped this would open the door to a broader political settlement of the crisis in the Balkan state.
